design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA; PROSPERO 42016052223) of observational studies comparing adults who use illicit methamphetamine or amphetamine with and without psychotic symptoms or disorder (MAP vs MNP) on sociodemographic, drug-use, psychiatric, family-history and trauma factors. 20 papers from 13 study populations (5476 participants as reported); 11 cross-sectional and 2 cohort designs. Quality rated with a modified Newcastle–Ottawa Scale built for the review; evidence for each factor graded with reference to GRADE; synthesis by narrative and counting of studies with and without a significant association.
can_establish: Which factors have been reported, and how often, as correlates of psychotic symptoms among people who use methamphetamine, and how weak the underlying study designs are.
cannot_establish: That any factor, including frequency of use, causes psychosis, or how large any association is across studies: there is no pooled estimate, most included studies are cross-sectional with lifetime outcomes, and the comparison is between users with and without psychosis, not between users and non-users.

sample.recruitment: Included populations came from community and dance-venue samples, needle-syringe programmes, outpatient and residential treatment, psychiatric inpatient units, detention centres and prison (Table 1): 4 in Asia (China, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia), 5 in Australia, 3 in the USA and 1 in Sweden (Results › Study characteristics, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults (>17 years) with illicit methamphetamine or amphetamine use in the past 12 months; users with current or lifetime psychotic symptoms compared with users without, psychosis measured by a validated instrument or structured interview; people with methamphetamine as primary drug analysed separately. Case reports, reviews and animal studies excluded (Method, 2nd paragraph; Study design and data extraction, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not summarized across studies; Table 1 gives setting, injecting proportion and exclusion of prior psychotic disorder per study.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Screening: 402 records, 45 duplicates removed, 320 excluded on title or abstract, 17 full texts excluded, 20 included (Abstract; Figure 1, an image, not read).
sample.selection_effects: Most populations come from treatment, needle-syringe, custodial or psychiatric settings with heavy use; the authors note these may not represent adults who use methamphetamine generally (Implications for future research, 3rd paragraph). By Table 1, seven populations did not exclude people with primary psychotic disorders (studies 1, 2, 5, 7, 9, 11, 12) and one did not screen systematically (study 10); the Discussion lists only five of these populations (Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: In the primary studies: self-reported frequency, amount, duration, age at onset and route of methamphetamine use; dependence by DSM-IV symptom counts or the Severity of Dependence Scale. No biological verification described. In 8 of 13 populations, current use was related to a lifetime psychosis outcome, so use and psychosis may refer to different times (Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Only six included papers (from five populations) adjusted for other drug use (Strengths and limitations, 4th paragraph). Alcohol dependence was associated with psychosis in 3 populations and frequent cannabis use in 1 (Table 2), so other drugs are both a confounder and a correlate.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Varied; not summarized. One included population required at least 3 weeks' abstinence (study 13, Table 1).

comparison.controls: Users without psychotic symptoms or disorder (MNP), within the same populations. No comparison with people who do not use methamphetamine.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Whether psychosis or its risk factors preceded methamphetamine use is generally unknown in the cross-sectional studies; the authors state that the literature is insufficient to support a causal association (Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Psychosis measures in the primary studies: BPRS (current, past month), a 7-item psychosis screen (past year), PRISM-IV, MINI, MINI-plus and DIGS-C (current or lifetime psychotic disorder), hospitalisation coded as substance-induced psychosis (registry), the Methamphetamine Experience Questionnaire (lifetime paranoia) and CIDI-based questions (Table 1 and notes).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality by a modified Newcastle–Ottawa Scale developed for this review (representativeness 3, risk-factor assessment 3, psychosis absent at start 2, comparability and confounding 2, outcome assessment 3; total 13), which the authors acknowledge is not validated (Quality assessment; Strengths and limitations, 1st paragraph). Per-study scores are in Table 3, an online appendix not read.
outcomes.operationalization: A factor counts as associated when a primary study reports a significant association; Table 2 sorts studies into 'association' and 'no association' rows (vote counting). Outcome-level certainty judged with reference to GRADE by two authors.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable at review level; not addressed. 22 factors were synthesized from primary studies that each tested many correlates.

analysis.effect_sizes: No meta-analysis: it was planned for factors reported in three or more studies with acceptable heterogeneity, but inconsistent reporting prevented it (Study synthesis). No pooled estimates, I², τ², prediction intervals or publication-bias tests. Estimates quoted from single studies: frequency of use, 3 to 11 times higher odds of psychosis across four studies (intervals not given except one); within-person, 16 or more days of use per month vs fewer, OR 11.2 (95% CI 5.9–21.1) (McKetin et al., 2013); dependence vs none, 2 to 3 times higher odds (Ding et al., 2014; Kalayasiri et al., 2009, 2014); family history of schizophrenia, OR 5.4 (95% CI 2.0–14.7) (Chen et al., 2003); three or more adverse childhood experiences, OR 4.5 (95% CI 1.6–12.6) (Ding et al., 2014); hospitalisation for substance-induced psychosis, education OR 0.8 (95% CI 0.7–1.0) and past-month homelessness OR 2.5 (95% CI 1.1–5.3) (Rognli et al., 2014) (Results, factor sections).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level. Moderators were discussed only qualitatively and at study level (current vs lifetime outcome, setting, East Asian populations for duration of use); no formal moderator analysis.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO 42016052223, registered before data extraction (whether before searching and screening is not stated). The protocol was updated to add a Google Scholar forward-citation search after reference-list screening found five further citations (Method, 1st and 4th paragraphs).
analysis.selective_reporting: Search: MEDLINE (Ovid), PsycINFO and Embase from inception to 8 December 2016, no language restriction, plus reference lists of earlier reviews and a forward-citation search; the main search required a 'risk factor' concept, and the supplementary searches found five further citations (Method, 3rd and 4th paragraphs). No grey literature or registries. Overlap: earlier narrative reviews (Bramness et al., 2012; Glasner-Edwards and Mooney, 2014; Rognli and Bramness, 2015; Bramness and Rognli, 2016) and a 2004 systematic review of stimulant psychosis (Curran et al.) cited in the Introduction. The synthesis omits two findings that Table 1 reports for study 4 (transient symptoms associated with male sex and earlier onset of use) from the gender and age-at-onset rows of Table 2.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Vote counting treats non-significant results in small samples as evidence of no association.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Frequency of use was associated with psychotic symptoms in four populations and not in four others; dependence was associated in four by the review's count, but Table 1 records one of those four (Ding et al., 2014) as finding no association with dependence. The review dismisses the null frequency studies as lifetime-outcome, recall-biased and lower quality, yet Table 1 shows two of the four (McKetin et al., 2010; Hides et al., 2015) related current psychosis to current use, and their quality ratings overlap those of the positive studies. The strongest evidence is one within-person cohort (McKetin et al., 2013; OR 11.2). Certainty was judged moderate for frequency and low to very low for every other factor, and the authors state the evidence is insufficient to support causation.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says frequency of use and severity of dependence were "consistently found to be associated with psychosis" (Abstract, Results), and the conclusion calls them the most consistent predictors (Conclusion). The Discussion reads the pattern as adding to the concept that greater use results in a greater likelihood of psychosis (Discussion, 1st paragraph) while the limitations section says causation is not supported (Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph). 'Consistently' does not describe a four-to-four split for frequency, the dependence count includes a study the review's own table lists as null, and the moderate certainty for frequency rests on upgrading for effect size and a dose–response gradient from a single study without downgrading for that inconsistency.

timeline.event: Narrative review of amphetamine-induced psychosis, cited here as one of three earlier reviews without systematic methods.

Prospective within-person cohort of people with methamphetamine dependence: odds of psychotic symptoms during months of 16 or more days of use OR 11.2 (95% CI 5.9–21.1) as quoted in this review; the basis of its moderate certainty for frequency.
Narrative review of methamphetamine psychosis, cited here as an earlier non-systematic review (and, apparently in error, in place of an included primary study; see reporting issues).
Later systematic review and meta-analysis of mental-health outcomes of amphetamine use, including psychosis; appraised in its own card.

replication.where_it_stands: The within-person, dose-related association between days of methamphetamine use and psychotic symptoms rests mainly on one prospective cohort; the cross-sectional literature is split and mostly measures lifetime outcomes. This review adds a structured inventory and a quality rating, not a pooled estimate.

funding.funder: Australian National Health and Medical Research Council postgraduate scholarship (Grant 1093778), a stipend to the first author during PhD candidature (Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: Dan Lubman has provided consultancy advice to Lundbeck and Indivior and received travel support and speaker honoraria from AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb, Janssen, Lundbeck and Servier. No other conflicts declared (Declaration of Conflicting Interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Turning Point, Eastern Health and Monash University (Arunogiri, Lubman); University of Otago (Foulds); National Drug Research Institute, Curtin University (McKetin). By the first three author names shown in the reference list, review authors co-authored at least included studies 1, 3, 4 and 5 (McKetin) and 1 and 4 (Lubman), including the cohort that carries the moderate rating; screening, extraction and quality rating were done by the two authors who were not on those studies (Arunogiri and Foulds). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant-data analysis, or new prospective cohorts, of people who use methamphetamine without prior psychotic disorder, with contemporaneous timeline follow-back of methamphetamine and other drug use (with biological checks), repeated structured psychosis assessments, within-person analysis adjusted for cannabis and alcohol, and pre-registered definitions of each risk factor.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Items 11, 12 and 15 do not apply because no meta-analysis was performed. One critical flaw (no list of excluded full texts) with several non-critical weaknesses gives low confidence under AMSTAR 2. Confidence in the headline conclusions is further reduced by internal inconsistencies in how studies were counted for frequency and dependence (see reporting issues), which AMSTAR 2 does not score directly.

key_findings.finding: Search of MEDLINE (Ovid), PsycINFO and Embase from inception to 8 December 2016 without language restriction, plus reference lists and a forward-citation search; 402 records screened, 20 papers from 13 populations included, 5476 participants as reported.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Method, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Results › Study characteristics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Sample sizes in Table 1 sum to 5472; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Eleven of 13 populations were studied cross-sectionally; five measured current psychosis (studies 1–5) and eight lifetime disorder or symptoms (studies 6–13).

Quality scores on the modified Newcastle–Ottawa Scale ranged from 5 to 12 of 13 (mean 7.85, SD 2.08); the commonest weaknesses were failure to exclude pre-existing psychotic disorder and insufficient control for other drug use. Only one population (McKetin et al., 2013) was rated in the top band.
key_findings.locator: Risk of bias within studies; Table 1

key_findings.finding: No meta-analysis was possible; synthesis was narrative, by counting studies with and without a significant association.

Frequency of use: associated with psychosis in four populations (McKetin et al., 2006, 2013; Ding et al., 2014; Kalayasiri et al., 2009), with odds 3 to 11 times higher in more frequent users; not associated in four (Glasner-Edwards et al., 2008; Hides et al., 2015; McKetin et al., 2010; Rognli et al., 2014). Rated the only factor with moderate certainty.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dose-amount and frequency of MA use; Table 2; Risk of bias across studies

key_findings.finding: In the one prospective within-person cohort, months with 16 or more days of use carried higher odds of psychotic symptoms than months with fewer, OR 11.2 (95% CI 5.9–21.1), with adjustment for other drug use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Dose-amount and frequency of MA use

key_findings.finding: Severity of dependence: associated in four populations by the review's count (dependent vs non-dependent odds 2 to 3 times higher), not associated in one (Hides et al., 2015).
key_findings.locator: Results › Severity of MA dependence; Table 2
key_findings.note: Table 1 lists Ding et al. (2014), one of the four, as not associated with dependence.

key_findings.finding: Amount of use was associated in three of four populations, all with lifetime outcomes; route of use (injecting) was not associated in any of four; age at onset and years of use gave inconsistent results.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Duration; Route of MA use

key_findings.finding: Sociodemographic factors (age, sex, employment, income, education) were generally not associated; one registry cohort found fewer years of schooling (OR 0.8, 95% CI 0.7–1.0) and recent homelessness (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.1–5.3) associated with hospitalisation for substance-induced psychosis.
key_findings.note: Table 1 reports that in study 4 transient symptoms were associated with male sex, which the gender row of Table 2 omits.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol dependence was associated with psychosis in three populations and frequent cannabis use in one; antisocial personality or conduct disorder in four; current major depression in three; family history of schizophrenia in one (OR 5.4, 95% CI 2.0–14.7); three or more adverse childhood experiences in one (OR 4.5, 95% CI 1.6–12.6).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Other drug use, Personality factors, Family history, Trauma

key_findings.finding: Certainty was low to very low for all factors except frequency of use; the authors state the literature is insufficient to support a causal association.
key_findings.locator: Risk of bias across studies; Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph; Table 2 footnote b

key_findings.finding: Only six included papers adjusted for other drug use.

The Introduction cites a prevalence of psychotic symptoms of 15–23% among people using methamphetamine in community settings and up to 60% among dependent users in treatment; the Discussion cites up to 30% transition to persistent psychotic illness in longitudinal studies.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Strengths and limitations, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: Background figures from cited studies, not results of this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists Ding et al. (2014) as not associated with methamphetamine dependence, but Table 2 counts it among the four studies in which dependence was associated with psychosis, and the text uses it for the 2-to-3-fold odds.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 (study 9); Table 2 (Dependence); Results › Severity of MA dependence
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'consistent' dependence association may rest on three populations, all rated in the lowest quality band (studies 2, 11 and 12).

reporting_issues.issue: The null frequency studies are described as having measured lifetime psychosis (Table 2 comment) and three of them as reporting lifetime substance-induced psychotic disorder (text), but Table 1 shows McKetin et al. (2010) used a current (past-year) screen and Hides et al. (2015) related current psychotic disorder to current use; Rognli et al. (2014) used hospitalisation during follow-up.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 2 (Frequency); Results › Dose-amount and frequency of MA use; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The reason given for discounting the null studies, and hence for the moderate certainty rating, is not supported by the review's own table.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that studies finding a frequency association were of higher quality is followed by a citation list that includes Chen et al. and Sulaiman et al., which are not among the four frequency-positive studies; by the Table 1 bands, positive studies (+, ++, ++, +++) and null studies (+, ++, ++, +) differ only by the single top-band study.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Dose-amount and frequency of MA use; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The quality argument rests on one study.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 totals do not match Table 1 sample sizes: study 3 behaves as N=79 in every total (Table 1 prints 75; overall 5476 vs a Table 1 sum of 5472); the gender row says 6 studies but cites 7; the polydrug 'association' row cites studies 8 and 12 but its N (268) equals studies 3 and 9, which Table 1 lists with polydrug or other drug use as correlates (study 8 also appears in the 'no association' row); totals for frequency 'no association' (2503 vs 2508–2512), dependence 'association' (1577 vs 1450) and family history 'association' (912 vs 723) cannot be reproduced from the cited studies (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Participant counts per factor are unreliable; cite the primary studies for numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: Among studies finding no association with use variables, the text cites Glasner-Edwards and Mooney (2014), a narrative review, instead of the included study (Glasner-Edwards et al., 2008).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Results › Patterns of MA use, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion lists seven papers (five populations) as not excluding primary psychotic disorders, but Table 1 records three further populations that did not exclude them (studies 1, 5 and 7), including one of the frequency-positive studies (McKetin et al., 2006, in which 10% had a previous psychotic disorder).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Contamination by primary psychosis is understated, including in evidence for the frequency association.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 reports that in study 4 transient symptoms were associated with male sex and earlier onset of use, yet the text states that sex was not associated in any study and Table 2 omits study 4 from the gender and age-at-onset rows.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 (study 4); Results › Sociodemographic factors; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Findings from the highest-quality study are left out of the synthesis for two factors.

reporting_issues.issue: Quality bands overlap: '+' is defined as a total of 0–6 and '++' as 6–10.
reporting_issues.consequence: A score of 6 cannot be placed; minor.
